papers.title: From evidence to practice: Expert consensus for sleep dysfunction in Parkinson disease.
papers.abstract: Our Parkinson disease sleep recommendations provide an evidence-informed, expert consensus framework rather than a rigid treatment hierarchy. Emphasizing individualized risk-benefit assessment and practical point-of-care guidance, we address therapeutic decisions where definitive evidence is lacking while strongly supporting rigorous prospective trials to advance care.

papers.title: Glial handling of alpha-synuclein seeds: uptake, degradation and redistribution in pathological propagation.
papers.abstract: α-synuclein (αS) aggregation and propagation are central features of Parkinson's disease pathology. Preformed fibril (PFF) models have shown that extracellular αS aggregates can enter neurons and seed aggregation of endogenous αS. Within the brain, these seeds also encounter microglia and astrocytes, which efficiently internalise fibrillar αS and can influence its subsequent fate. This review examines the mechanisms through which glial cells take up, process, degrade and redistribute extracellular αS seeds. When lysosomal trafficking and degradation are effective, glia can act as a sink for seed-competent αS and restrict neuronal seeding and propagation. In contrast, lysosomal dysfunction, incomplete proteolysis or excessive aggregate burden can promote persistence, modification and redistribution of seed-competent αS, including through extracellular vesicles and intercellular transfer. Evidence from microglial and astrocytic models therefore indicates that the outcome of glial uptake depends on the balance between internalisation, intracellular processing and subsequent release. Differences in αS conformation, fibril preparation, inflammatory state, genetic background and experimental model may further explain the apparently protective and pathogenic effects of glia reported across different studies. Understanding the factors that determine whether glial uptake results in productive clearance or continued propagation may identify therapeutic strategies that enhance the removal of pathogenic αS without broadly suppressing glial function.

papers.title: Effects of Fecal Microbiota Transplantation on Inflammatory Markers in Parkinson's Disease: Exploratory Results from the EFFACE-PD Study.
papers.abstract: Inflammation and gut dysbiosis are increasingly recognized as important contributors to the pathophysiology of Parkinson's disease (PD). Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) has emerged as a potential therapeutic strategy aimed at restoring gut microbial balance and modulating inflammatory pathways. The aim of the study was to evaluate the effect of single fecal microbiota transplantation on systemic and gut-related inflammatory biomarkers in patients with PD. This exploratory analysis was conducted as part of the randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled EFFACE-PD study. Fifty-nine participants with PD were randomized to receive either donor-derived FMT or placebo. Serum levels of IL-18 and calprotectin were measured using ELISA before intervention and 3 months after the procedure. Ferritin, leukocyte count, neutrophils, lymphocytes, and neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) were assessed at baseline and after twelve months. No statistically significant between-group differences in changes in inflammatory biomarker concentrations were observed. Broader inflammatory markers, including ferritin and leukocyte parameters, also did not differ significantly between groups. We conclude that single FMT did not induce significant changes in systemic inflammatory biomarkers in this exploratory cohort of PD patients. Larger studies with standardized inflammatory assessments are needed to clarify the immunomodulatory effects of FMT in PD.

papers.title: Neuropharmacology of omega-3 long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids in neurodegenerative diseases: mechanisms, multi-omics evidence, and clinical translation.
papers.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, involve progressive neuronal dysfunction associated with neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, mitochondrial impairment, defective proteostasis, and synaptic failure. Although symptomatic treatment remains central, anti-amyloid therapies can modestly slow clinical decline in selected patients with early Alzheimer's disease. This review critically evaluates the neuropharmacological evidence for omega-3 long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids, particularly docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) and eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA), and the barriers to their clinical translation. We narratively synthesized preclinical, observational, and interventional clinical evidence, focusing on membrane organization, inflammatory resolution, mitochondrial and redox homeostasis, autophagy, proteostasis, neuronal signaling, and factors contributing to heterogeneous clinical outcomes. Preclinical studies support context-dependent effects of DHA and EPA on neuronal membranes, inflammatory signaling, mitochondrial function, redox balance, autophagy, and synaptic plasticity. Human evidence is less consistent: observational studies generally report favorable associations between omega-3 status and neurological outcomes, whereas randomized trials show null, modest, or subgroup-dependent effects. Outcomes vary with disease stage, baseline omega-3 status, formulation, dose, treatment duration, genotype, and endpoint selection. Uncertain central nervous system exposure and limited pharmacokinetic and target-engagement data remain major translational barriers. Omega-3 long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids are biologically plausible neuropharmacological modulators, but current evidence does not establish DHA or EPA as broadly effective disease-modifying treatments for neurodegenerative diseases. papers.title: Isolation and Functional Screening of Plant-Derived Natural Products for Assessing Healthy Aging and Neuroprotective Activities in Caenorhabditis elegans.
papers.abstract: Plant-derived natural products are a rich source of bioactive molecules with potential benefits for healthy aging and neuroprotection. Identifying compounds with these activities requires integrated platforms capable of evaluating multiple aspects of organismal health. Caenorhabditis elegans provides a genetically tractable, physiologically conserved in vivo model ideally suited for functional screening of natural products. This protocol presents a comprehensive workflow for preparing plant extracts, characterizing their antioxidant properties, and assessing their effects on stress resistance, healthspan, lifespan, and neuroprotective effects in C. elegans. Methods begin with plant extraction and routine maintenance of nematode and bacterial cultures to ensure consistency across experiments. Antioxidant activity is assessed through oxidative stress resistance assays, intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) quantification, stress-responsive reporter activation, and subcellular localization of the transcription factors DAF-16/FOXO and SKN-1/Nrf2. Healthspan assessments include lipofuscin accumulation, pharyngeal pumping, reproductive function, growth, and locomotion. Longevity effects are determined using lifespan assays. Neuroprotective potential is examined in models of β-amyloid/tau toxicity, chemotaxis impairment, polyglutamine aggregation, and α-synuclein aggregation relevant to Alzheimer's, Huntington's, and Parkinson's diseases. Collectively, this platform enables systematic functional screening of plant-derived natural products and supports the discovery of compounds that promote stress resistance, improve healthspan, and mitigate proteotoxic neurodegeneration.

papers.title: Differentiation of PD, MSA and PSP using clinical data from the prospective AIDP cohort.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Differentiation of clinical features among Parkinson's disease (PD), progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), and multiple system atrophy parkinsonism (MSAp) is challenging, with a paucity of comparative studies on comprehensive and overlapped clinical features across three of them. OBJECTIVE: Comprehensive data from the Automated Imaging Differentiation for Parkinsonism (AIDP) study could offer valuable insights into their diagnostic differentiation among PD, PSP and MSAp. METHODS: Demographics, comprehensive motor and non-motor features, daily living function and quality of life (QoL) data were prospectively collected from individuals with PD, probable PSP, and probable MSAp at their second AIDP study visit. Clinical diagnoses were confirmed independently by three movement disorder neurologists. Cross-sectional group comparisons were conducted using Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise tests. Median and logistic regression models were applied to assess differences, adjusting for age, sex, disease duration and levodopa equivalent dosage. RESULTS: Among 168 individuals (90 PD, 56 probable PSP, 22 probable MSAp), overall motor, non-motor, daily living functions and QoL measures were found to be more impaired in MSAp and PSP than PD. Individuals with PSP experienced more oculomotor and cognitive impairment than PD and MSAp. Systolic and diastolic orthostatic blood pressure (BP) drop, orthostatic lightheadedness, and urinary incontinence were associated with MSAp. The presence of systolic orthostatic BP drop was also against the diagnosis of PSP. There were no differences in anxiety, depression, fatigue and constipation across three parkinsonism subtypes. CONCLUSION: Distinct impairments across PD, PSP, and MSAp in this well-characterized, prospectively collected, comprehensive motor and non-motor dataset provide valuable information for clinical differentiation.

papers.title: Enhanced functional connectivity in right precuneus after high-frequency repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation in Parkinson's disease patients with chronic musculoskeletal pain.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) can relieve chronic musculoskeletal pain (MSP) in Parkinson's disease (PD), yet the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. METHODS: In this double-blind, sham-controlled trial, 43 PD patients with MSP were randomly assigned to received 10 sessions of neuronavigated 10-Hz rTMS (n=22) or sham stimulation (n=21) over the bilateral primary motor cortex (M1). Clinical assessments were performed at baseline (T0), after the tenth session (T1), and at 1-month (T2) and 3-month (T3) follow-up; functional MRI (fMRI) was acquired at T0 and T1. RESULTS: In the rTMS group, compared to T0, King's Parkinson's Disease Pain Scale (KPPS) and Visual Analog Scale scores decreased significantly at T1, T2, and T3 (p < 0.05). MDS-Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (MDS-UPDRS) III, Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (HAMA), Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HAMD), and Parkinson's Disease Sleep Scale (PDSS) scores were significantly lower at T1 and T2 than at T0 (p < 0.05), but not at T3 (p > 0.05). No significant correlations were found between KPPS and MDS-UPDRS III, HAMA, HAMD, or PDSS scores (p > 0.05) alterations in the rTMS group. fMRI revealed that patients exhibited decreased amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations in the left cuneus and enhanced functional connectivity between the left cuneus and the right precuneus after rTMS treatment. The sham group showed no significant changes in clinical scores or fMRI. CONCLUSIONS: High-frequency rTMS over bilateral M1 was associated with improvement of MSP in PD, accompanied by reduced local neural activity in the left cuneus and enhanced connectivity between the left cuneus and the right precuneus. These findings are preliminary and hypothesis generating.

papers.title: Differential effects of dopaminergic medication and subthalamic deep brain stimulation on gait in Parkinson's disease: A two-case report.
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: In Parkinson's disease (PD), interactions between medication (Med) and deep brain stimulation (DBS) across gait domains and in individuals with distinct clinical profiles remain incompletely understood. This study conducted detailed within-subject gait analyses in two individuals with PD across four conditions: (1) DBS ON/Med ON, (2) DBS OFF/Med ON, (3) DBS ON/Med OFF, and (4) DBS OFF/Med OFF, comparing results with healthy reference data. CASE 1: Due to fluctuations in effectiveness that could no longer be treated with oral medication, accompanied by pronounced dyskinesia and insufficient tremor control, decision for subthalamic nucleus (STN) stimulator implantation was made. The patient continued to receive medication. STN-DBS primarily optimized axial control and intersegmental coordination, substantially increasing walking speed, while dopaminergic medication provided limited additional benefit. CASE 2: The patient noticed increasing bradykinesia of the left leg, later accompanied by rigidity and resting tremor, and subsequently on the right side. He suffered from severe freezing episodes. Under dopamine agonists, he experienced nightmares and pseudohallucinations. Thus, STN stimulator implantation was performed. The patient continued to receive medication. STN-DBS improved posture and alignment, bringing kinematics closer to those of healthy controls, while the effects of combined STN-DBS and medication appeared more complementary than in Case 1. CONCLUSION: Results demonstrated differential and partially complementary effects of medication and stimulation across gait domains. Clinically, inter-individual variability should be considered. The DBS ON/Med ON condition did not consistently provide maximal improvement across all outcomes, highlighting the value of comprehensive gait assessment for individualized therapy optimization.

papers.title: Education, MoCA-Defined Baseline Cognitive Status, and Screening-Level Cognitive Change After Bilateral Subthalamic Nucleus Deep Brain Stimulation in Parkinson's Disease: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Cognitive outcomes after subthalamic nucleus deep brain stimulation (STN-DBS) in Parkinson's disease (PD) remain variable. Whether education, a proxy for cognitive reserve, is associated with postoperative MoCA-based cognitive performance is uncertain. METHODS: This retrospective cohort included 111 patients with PD who underwent bilateral STN-DBS from 2015 to 2024 and had paired Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) data. Patients were classified as MoCA-defined mild cognitive impairment (MCI; baseline MoCA ≤ 21; n RESULTS: In unadjusted analyses, mean MoCA increased modestly overall (+0.9 ± 4.5; p CONCLUSIONS: Group-level MoCA-based cognitive screening performance showed no overall deterioration after bilateral STN-DBS. The greater unadjusted increase among patients with lower baseline MoCA scores should be interpreted cautiously because baseline-score effects may contribute. Education may provide useful adjunctive information for cognitive risk assessment but cannot replace comprehensive neuropsychological evaluation.

papers.title: Longevity of Non-Rechargeable Implantable Pulse Generators in Deep Brain Stimulation: A Systematic Review.
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: The longevity of non-rechargeable implantable pulse generator (IPG) is an important consideration in deep brain stimulation (DBS), as battery depletion may cause loss of therapeutic benefit, and repeated replacement exposes patients to cumulative surgical morbidity. We aimed to systematically evaluate non-rechargeable DBS IPG longevity, determinants of battery life, comparative device performance, and clinical consequences of battery depletion and replacement. METHODS: PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched from inception to 2 August 2026. Original human studies reporting non-rechargeable IPG longevity, depletion or replacement, energy consumption, or related clinical outcomes were included; rechargeable IPGs were considered separately. RESULTS: Of 1,476 initial records, 30 studies were included, with reported sample sizes totalling 4,101 observations. Observed non-rechargeable IPG longevity ranged from approximately 2 to >6 years. In a single cohort stratified by indication, longevity was shortest in dystonia (37.0±2.0 months), intermediate in Parkinson's disease (51.5±2.3 months), and longest in essential tremor (71.9±6.7 months), although disease, target, and stimulation requirements were closely interrelated. Higher stimulation-energy demand, including greater amplitude, pulse width, frequency, and total electrical energy delivered (TEED), was consistently associated with shorter longevity. Direct comparisons also demonstrated clinically important differences in longevity between generations of non-rechargeable IPGs, independent of stimulation-energy demand in some cohorts. Major infection occurred after 30 replacements (2.3%), and each previous replacement increased infection odds (OR 1.6). Depletion-associated parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome resulted in 2 deaths. papers.title: Identifying Exploratory Physical Activity Thresholds Associated With Symptom Severity in Older Adults With Parkinson's Disease.
papers.abstract: This research identified exploratory physical activity (PA) thresholds associated with symptom severity in older adults with Parkinson's disease and assessed their association with cardiometabolic and cognitive health. Data were collected from 3,259 participants (age: 65.64 ± 10.37) in the Fox Insight database. PA was measured using Physical Activity Scale for the Elderly. Quadratic regression identified exploratory PA thresholds for managing motor, nonmotor, and depressive symptoms, with minimum thresholds based on literature-defined cut points and optimal thresholds based on symptom plateaus. Logistic regression assessed relationship between these thresholds and prevalence of hypertension, diabetes, and mild cognitive impairment. Analyses identified exploratory minimum and optimal Physical Activity Scale for the Elderly threshold of 150 and 245. Meeting minimum PA threshold was associated with lower odds of hypertension (21.1%), diabetes (40.6%), and mild cognitive impairment (57.9%; p < .01). These findings provide evidence-based exploratory PA thresholds to guide future research on PA patterns in older adults with Parkinson's disease.
